newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil scandal won't hurt re-election bill-Cardoso.
newsitem.headline: Brazil scandal won't hurt re-election bill-Cardoso.

text.p: A new corruption scandal in Congress will be investigated, but will not affect the progress of a bill that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election next year, a presidential spokesman said.
"The president had absolutely no knowledge of these allegations and he considers them to be serious. They have to investigated," spokesman Sergio Amaral told reporters.

Newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo Tuesday published details of what it said was a taped telephone conversation in which deputy Ronivon Santiago allegedly says he and four other lawmakers received up to $188,000 to vote for the re-election bill.
The payments were made by the governors of Acre and Amazonas states, Folha said.
Amaral said the Chamber of Deputies would set up an internal inquiry to look into the allegations, but added there was no need to put on hold the re-election bill which is now in the Senate.
"There is no reason at all why the re-election bill should be suspended," he said.

Earlier Tuesday, a Senate committee mulling the re-election bill delayed until Wednesday a session which might include a vote on the reform, but defeated an opposition motion which would have suspended the vote indefinitely.
Amaral also denied long-standing opposition claims that the government traded favors in exchange for support in Congress for the re-election bill.
"The government repudiates any deal-making over its reforms," the spokesman said. "Where in the Offical Gazette is there any evidence of the government giving in to win votes?"
Amaral was referring to Brazil's official journal in which appointments to government posts and other decrees are formally announced.
